label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here's the letter. I kept it in your voice — the bits you told me are all in there, and I tried to leave room for a few laughs even in the middle of the sappy parts. Denise can read it straight through; I'd only ask her to pause before the pager story so Nana gets the laugh properly.

---

**Nana,**

It's Friday night, the night before the move. Denise is sitting in your kitchen reading this out loud, which is a strange thing to write and an even stranger thing to hear, but I wanted you to have it in a letter instead of a phone call, so here we are.

I've started this about six times this week. Every time I got to a certain part I'd choke up and close the laptop and go look at something meaningless on the internet instead. So I'm going to just say the important thing first, before I lose my nerve again, and then I'll tell you the rest.

**I'm proud of you.** Not the kind of proud people say when somebody's had a sad year. The other kind — the kind where somebody did a hard thing and didn't make a fuss about it and didn't ask anybody's permission. You looked at that house on Kathleen Street, you looked at Elmwood Terrace, and you picked Elmwood. You picked it. Nobody made you do it, nobody nudged you, you just decided. I want that said out loud tonight, in the kitchen, because you should hear it from somebody who means it.

Denise, if you get to that part and your voice goes, just keep going. She won't mind. She pretends to mind.

**The house.**

Fifty-one years. You and Walt moved in fifty-one years ago and that kitchen has been the whole family's headquarters ever since. I know I wasn't there for most of it, but I know what that room did. It raised half of us. That's not a small thing for a room to do. Other people have houses. That house had a kitchen, and the kitchen had a table, and the table had whoever needed sitting at it that week — us, cousins, the neighbours' kids, everybody. My own two cousins learned to tie their shoes at that table, and I promise you that table takes more credit for how our family turned out than I do.

Walt would have had an opinion about the move. He would have said something about how it was only a box or two, and then he would have carried three of them anyway and complained about the stairs. I wish he could have been here for it. He would have liked Elmwood, I think. He would have said the parking lot was "fine."

**The summers.**

I want to tell you about the little TV in the kitchen, because I don't think anybody else remembers it the way I do. It was small enough that you had to sit slightly forward, and it sat on that shelf by the window, and it was on for the Expos and the Jays. You let me stay up and watch if I dried the dishes. I want to be clear about the exchange rate: I dried every dish in that kitchen, including the ones you only soaked, and I did it for a whole summer, and I never once thought about haggling. In hindsight that was a bad deal for you. I would have watched you fold laundry.

And I was on the back steps with you at six in the morning. You with your tea, me half asleep in a t-shirt, the whole street still asleep. You never said a word until the cup was done. Every single morning. I've thought about that more than I should have for a man my age. I'm not going to try to explain what that was, because you'd tell me to go back to my tea, and you were right.

**Crib.**

You taught me when I was seven. You handed me the board and the cards and you did not go easy on me. You never once let me win, and I want to say that plainly, because it's the best thing anybody has ever done for me: you didn't let me win, and you didn't let me quit either. Both of those were gifts and I didn't know it until I was older.

I skunked you when I was fifteen. Fifteen. You handed over the money — or you didn't, depending on whether you were in a good mood — and then you went and made me a whole pan of butter tarts. A whole pan. Not two. A pan. And I sat at that table and ate them and I think about it maybe once a week, Nana. I was fifteen and I'd won, and the whole point of it was the butter tarts afterwards. That's the deal. That's always been the deal.

I don't know if you know this, but I still play. Not as much. Badly, some of the time, and mostly with guys who let me win, which is a completely different experience and honestly a waste of a Tuesday.

**The twenty dollar bill.**

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a card with a twenty dollar bill taped inside it and the words, "for pizza, you look thin on the computer."

I want you to know that bill went through a postal system and a bank and it is still, to this day, taped inside a card, and it is in a drawer in my apartment, and I am not going to throw it out. I have moved apartments twice. It came with me both times.

I also want it on the record that you were right. That was the summer. That was the exact moment. "You look thin on the computer" is the most accurate thing anybody has ever said about me, including my doctor.

**Did anything break.**

Okay, here's the thing. My pager went off at your table last Christmas. Right in the middle of dinner. It was the worst technology ever invented by human beings and I was the one holding it, and it went off, and you put your fork down and asked me if the internet was broken again.

*Again.*

Nana. It was a pager. There was no internet involved. There was no internet to break. But you were not wrong to ask, because honestly, in my line of work, something is always breaking. That's the entire job. I get paid a good amount of money to make sure things don't break, and I have been doing it for a decade, and you are still the only person who checks.

So let me answer it the way you like it answered: no. Nothing's broken. Nothing's ever broken. Your house is not broken, your internet is not broken, and when the movers show up tomorrow morning and the whole place gets upside down, it's not broken, it's just backwards for a day. You'll survive it. You've moved before.

And if you want to know the truth, you're the reason I can say that. You taught me that if you check on a thing, it'll be fine. I've been checking on things ever since. I'm very good at it now. You'd be proud of how good I am at it.

**Elmwood.**

I've seen the pictures. It looks nice, and I want to be clear, because I know what people say when somebody in your situation moves into a place like this — they say "it's a nice place" like it's a consolation prize. It's not a consolation prize. It's the second floor, and the room looks out at a parking lot and a big maple, and the maple is going to turn in the fall and in a couple of years it's going to be doing that thing where it just dumps everything at once and the whole parking lot is orange. You're going to know that maple. You're going to know that parking lot. You're going to know which car belongs to whom and which one leaves at 7:15 and which one parks badly on purpose.

Second floor. There's a fire escape, Nana. I'm going to find it when I come up on the 5th, and we're going to go out on it with two cups of tea at six in the morning, and you can tell me about the neighbours' cars. I won't say anything until your cup is done. I know the rules.

And Nana — they've got a crib league.

I said it. I know. I know what you're thinking and I know what you're already planning. You're going to be in that league before your boxes are unpacked. You're going to be the one they have to be nice to, because you're going to beat them, because that's what you do. Those church ladies on Tuesdays have no idea what's coming. Please do not go easy on anybody in that league. You never went easy on me.

**Denise is bringing the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest.** Good. The cedar chest has the good blankets in it, so that has to come. And the clock — Denise, wind it before you leave, and if it chimes at three in the morning in a strange new room, that's how it says hello.

And I got the crib board. I've had it for a while, actually. It was sitting in my closet in a moving box with my old running shoes, and it looked like it needed out of there, and honestly, so did I. It's coming up on the 5th. I've got it in the car in December. That's not a joke.

**The other thing.**

I want to talk about the fact that I'm not there tomorrow, and I'm not going to do it the way people usually do it, where they say "it's fine, don't worry about it" in a voice that makes everybody in the room worry about it.

It isn't nothing. I'd have liked to be there. I'd have liked to carry something, and carry the wrong thing, and say "is that heavy?" and have you say "obviously it's heavy, are you new." I'd have liked to be there for the last morning, the one where you're standing in the kitchen not saying anything because there's nothing to say, and you look around and it's all just stuff.

But you're not doing it alone. You've got Denise, and you've got the movers, and you have been alone in that house for six years and you have not had a single day of trouble in it, and you are the single most prepared person I have ever met, including everyone I work with, and I work with people who get paid to be prepared. So I'll be fine, and you'll be fine, and Saturday morning is just a Saturday with a truck in front of it.

And when I call you on Sunday, which I will, you're going to answer, and I'm going to ask how the move went, and you're going to tell me it went fine, and then you're going to ask me if anything broke.

Nothing broke, Nana. Nothing's broken.

I'm coming up on the morning of the 5th, as soon as my rotation's done, which means I will be at Elmwood Terrace with a crib board under my arm and probably a box of butter tarts in the other hand, because I don't know how to show up anywhere empty-handed and I've never learned.

You pick the spot. You always picked the spot. Put the board on the table by the window, where you can see the maple, and we'll deal a hand. Your first game in the new place, with the old board, in the room you picked, in the life you decided you wanted.

I've got a lot of years of Tuesdays to catch up on.

Love you, Nana. See you on the 5th.

**— your grandson**

---

One small suggestion: have Denise read the butter tart line and the "the internet was broken *again*" line a beat slower — those are your two guaranteed laughs, and a half-second pause before them is worth more than any wording change. Everything else she can just read as it comes.
